title: Amplitude-Defect Mediated Transition to Partial Incoherence -- From Experiment to Theory
authors: Nicolas Thomé, Yukiteru Murakami, Yannick Schöhs, Katharina Krischer
abstract: Phase-only models have contributed significantly to the understanding of synchronization; however, they do not account for dynamical scenarios where amplitude dynamics matter. This study identifies an amplitude-mediated transition from complete frequency coherence to partial incoherence, observed both in an electrochemical silicon-etching experiment and within a population of globally coupled heterogeneous Stuart-Landau oscillators. Strong coupling introduces a bimodal-amplitude distribution from which the transition to partial incoherence is triggered by successive secondary Hopf bifurcations in low-amplitude oscillators. When these modulations cause oscillators to experience amplitude defects, the winding number changes, converting the secondary frequency into a new, oscillator-specific mean frequency. This mechanism results in a partially incoherent state, in which one amplitude group maintains frequency locking while another develops a dispersed frequency branch. These findings demonstrate that amplitude defects offer a pathway to incoherence that phase-only models cannot capture.
summary: The paper analyzes the transition from synchronized coherence to partial incoherence in coupled nonlinear oscillators, using both electrochemical experiments and theoretical models based on Stuart-Landau equations. The key finding is that this transition is mediated by amplitude defects arising from Hopf bifurcations in low-amplitude components. This mechanism proves that simple phase descriptions are insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of frequency dispersion.
main_problem: The study investigates a transition from complete frequency coherence to partial incoherence, demonstrating that this process is mediated by amplitude defects in a way that phase-only models fail to capture.
main_result: The transition occurs when low-amplitude oscillators undergo successive Hopf bifurcations, causing an amplitude defect that shifts the mean frequency of one group while another remains locked, leading to partial incoherence.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (Ellipsomicroscopy on silicon etching) with theoretical analysis using globally coupled heterogeneous Stuart-Landau oscillators and linear stability theory.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by globally coupled heterogeneous Stuart-Landau oscillators, which are used to simulate the nonlinear feedback dynamics observed during electrochemical dissolution of silicon in fluoride electrolytes.
key_observables: Amplitude ($A$), Phase ($\phi$), Mean Frequency, Amplitude Modulation Frequency (Mod. Freq.), and the Participation Ratio (PR) derived from eigenvalue analysis.
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($K$) and illumination intensity ($I$); the transition is characterized by crossing critical coupling strengths ($K_{HB}$) leading to Hopf bifurcations.
main_assumptions: The theoretical analysis relies on linear stability theory applied in a rotating frame, assuming the existence of a well-defined frequency-locked state $X^*$.
figures_summary: Figures show experimental heatmaps tracking amplitude and phase across different illumination intensities; numerical/theoretical figures illustrate transitions from coherence to partial incoherence via Hopf bifurcations and winding number changes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the phenomenon experimentally (varying illumination intensity), then modeling it with coupled oscillators, and finally using advanced stability analysis (Hopf bifurcation, PR calculation) to pinpoint the mechanism of amplitude-defect mediated frequency shifts.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how non-amplitude degrees of freedom (i.e., amplitude dynamics) are crucial for describing complex collective behavior in nonlinear oscillators, which has parallels in driven quantum systems or interacting quantum media.
